opening: Through the first few weeks of this young season, a flag seems to fly on every play. It feels worse than it has ever been. Too often a team has a game-breaking play called back on a wishy washy flag or something that had no effect on the outcome of the play. Flags have always been part of the game, but they feel more prominent now than ever. It seems that week after week flags have more of an impact on the game and a bigger impact on the final score. Am I delusional? Am I groaning over issues I made up completely in my mind? Only one way to find out, I'm going to run through the numbers to see whether that feeling holds up or if I'm just a mental case.
timeline: Average penalties and penalty yards per game, for every regular-season game since 1999. Dotted lines mark a point of emphasis or a rule change
early:
I wish I had the data to go back to the 70's and the era of aggressive, smashmouth football, but the furthest back with play by play data is 1999, so that's where we'll begin. I'll use this as the reference point and baseline for penalties before the later points of emphasis and rule changes. Across these first few years, a game averaged 12.6 flags and 105 penalty yards. On offense, false starts and offensive holding were the most common calls accounting for about 5 penalties a game between them. On the defensive side, they drew only about 5 penalties total a game. Pass interference and offside were the most common on that side with about 1 of each per game. 

2001 was the quiet year in this stretch averaging 11.4 flags a game. This is the lowest rate of penalization in this stretch and it doesn't fall that far again until 2008. 

Then in 2002 the Texans joined and the league increased to the 32 clubs which is what it sits at to this day. That season averaged 12.9 flags a game which was an increase from the previous 2 seasons, but still lower than the 1999 season. It appeared that the extra club didn't appear to have an increase on the league as a whole, however, the Texans were the most penalized team in the league averaging 8.75 penalties a game which was about 2 penalties more than the league average.  

Interestingly enough, offensive pass interference bottomed out in 2002 with only 47 calls across the league, the fewest of any season .
contact:
Stay with me, because we gotta go back before we can go forward. In 1978 total scoring had dropped to 34.4 points per game, the lowest in the young history of the modern era of football. The NFL was also in possibly its most physically imposing era and it showed seeing that no receiver had surpassed 1,000 yards the previous season. This was in large part due to defenders "chucking" or bumping receivers down the whole field, disrupting their timing and making the passing game difficult to watch. In response to these two factors, the NFL introduced a new rule for illegal contact. This rule drew an imaginary line five yards past the line of scrimmage. A defender could still jam a receiver inside that window, however, any contact the defender made beyond those 5 yards and before the throw, was now flagged as illegal contact. 

Now let's fast-forward back to 2003. Specifically, the AFC Championship game between the Patriots and the Colts. During this game, New England's defensive backs, led by cornerback Ty Law, repeatedly jammed, held, and grabbed Indianapolis receivers Marvin Harrison and Brandon Stokley well beyond the legal 5-yard window. This led to disrupted and physically overwhelmed Colts quarterback Peyton Manning who threw four interceptions, three to Ty Law alone, and completed under 50% of his passes. Despite this physical play, not a single penalty was called. In fact, there were only 7 penalties called all game which were all pre-snap infractions. The Patriots won this game and then later on won the Superbowl this same year. 

In the early 2000s, offenses were beginning to stall yet again. Year over year, passing yards per game, average points per game, and total passing touchdowns were all down. So after the season, frustrated Colts general manager Bill Polian took to the league demanding more stringent officiating for illegal contact. His sentiments, along with league executives fears that a boring, low-scoring brand of football would cause fans and television networks to lose interest, caused them to reconsider. 

The league sent officials back to the rulebooks for a refresh of the 1978 rule, encouraging more flags to deter illegal downfield contact and hopefully increase passing yards per game. Throughout the 2004 season, the crews were told to throw more flags for illegal contact. This, in turn, caused illegal contact penalties to skyrocket from 49 call in 2003 to 123 in 2004, the most of any increase for one specific penalty season over season across this whole study.

While still high, illegal contact penalties dropped slightly to 112 in 2025, clearly still a point of emphasis for the season. Defensive holding was another call the NFL pointed at, it surprisingly decreased from 167 in 2003 to 149 in 2004, perhaps due to majority of the focus being on the illegal contact, but it quickly rebounded and increasing to a all time high at the time 197 in 2005.

It seems officials were more active all across the board as False Starts also reached an all time high of 849 in 2005. Due to a refresh of the rulebooks and this focus on illegal contact, the game total moved from 13.2 in 2003 to 13.9 in 2004, then finally 14.5 flags per game average in 2005. That 2005 rate is the highest mark of all time for a finished season.
quiet:
After the most penalized season in history, the competition committee spent the spring of 2006 on the flag count. Rich McKay, co-chair of the committee, said too many of the 850 false starts were minor twitches that changed absolutely nothing, and that officials had to actually see a hold before they threw a flag for it, not just a guy on the ground complaining. Following this discussion, owners passed about 15 rule changes mainly centered around safety rules including the low hit on the quarterback and a wider horse-collar foul. While the minor twitching change for false starts was never actually passed, that year, the crews got less flag happy and the number reduced anyway.

For the first time since 2001, the NFL saw a drop in flags season over season. The averages fell from 14.5 flags and 116 penalty yards per game in 2005 to 11.9 flags and 98 penalty yards per game in 2006. The biggest of these drops was the phantom holding calls where officials previously had thrown flags on plays they may not have specifically seen or when there was a player on the ground complaining that there was a missed call. Offensive holding plummeted from 701 to 473 penalties over the whole season, nearly a 33% drop from the previous year. False starts, defensive holding, offside, and illegal contact all dropped by at least 15% as well. When it was all settled and done, the league average for penalties across the board had dropped about 20%.

Clearly there was a substantial drop year over year, but that still wasn't good enough for the NFL. Mike Pereira, then VP of officiating, still thought that certain calls were called a  bit too frequently having negative impacts on the game. One such call was roughing the passer which gives the offense a free 15 yards and an automatic first down, negating whatever action happened during the play. He told officials to be a bit more strict with the call and stop calling roughing the passer when the defender's arms were extended and the contact was minimal. Sure if a defender slammed the QB to the ground after the play, that is still very clearly roughing the passer, but if a defender just gives a little push after the ball was released, it was not worth calling a foul.  These calls dropped from the previous 3 years of 125, 116, and 95 penalties to 58 roughing the passer calls across all 90 games played that year. It stayed low that following season at only 57 before beginning to climb again and eventually sitting around 85-100 on an average year. 

At the behest of the league competition committee, these new rule changes and intentional effort to "let them play" caused 2008 to be the least penalized year in modern history. It was almost on par with the 2007 season, except it had seen a large reduction in false starts by nearly 100 penalties across the whole season. All the other initiatives to reduce penalties were still being focused on as points of emphasis and thus, penalties hovered at or around the previous years enforcement numbers.

This obviously didn't go unnoticed and Pereira sent the officiating staff to go back and review the games from the previous year and see what was being missed or ignored. The findings of this review concluded that they were way too lenient on holding, particularly with hooks and takedowns that seemed all too commonly uncalled. This review found 177 calls of these sorts that had not been called, so going forward, the crews should be more observant of these types of holds and throw a flag when appropriate. Additionally in this meeting, crews were told to enforce more player safety penalties such as not lunging at QBs as they were going out of bounds, no blindside blocking (RIP here come the boom edits), not hitting a defenseless receiver, and a reminded focus on horse collar tackles. 

To no surprise, penalties per game rose in 2009 and almost every type of penalty saw an uptick in calls. However, it seems that despite the flags flying more frequently, some players still were not getting the message through their heads about ensuring player safety. In an attempt to combat this, the NFL began giving out hefty fines for hits to the head or neck and threatened to suspend players who continuously showed no remorse for the hard hitting playstyle. The one player who probably comes to everyone's mind from this time period is James Harrison. He was one of the hardest hitting linebackers in the league on one of the most aggressive defenses in the league. During his time with the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2010, Harrison racked up quite the bill for fines totaling upwards of $125,000. 

The league continued to focus on player safety and had a few more initiatives centered around blows to the head, runners giving themselves up, forcible contact with the crown of the helmet, and taunting (Welcome to the No Fun League) to name a few. While the average penalties per game had a slight dip during the end of this era, it was more of a transition of penalties from one to another. This meant  rises in unnecessary roughness, holding, defensive pass interference, and defensive holding and decreases in false starts, defensive offsides, illegal contact, and illegal blocks. None the less, when the dust settled, the NFL had almost returned to that early 2000s baseline that was the precedence with around 12-12.5 penalties per game. So we're back to normal and since 2013 penalties have been the same right?
plateau:
Of course a new point of emphasis is where we start as it wriggled its way into the new 2014 season. This emphasis came on the back of a legendary defense, the Legion of Boom, who were coming off of a fresh Superbowl win. The Seahawks had one of the most dominant defenses in history and a lot of it can be attributed to their physicality. They were known for hard hits, superstars across the field, and you better not try the best corner in the game with any sorry receivers (Michael Crabtree perhaps?). In 2014 Dean Blandino, then new Vice President of officiating, pointed crews at this physical downfield contact on both sides of the ball. The Seahawks' secondary had spent the year grabbing receivers along their whole route and often times at or around the catch point. This was yet another re-emphasis to contact down field similar to that of 2004, a defender could still jam a receiver inside five yards, but past that imaginary line, contact that broke up or disrupted the route was illegal contact, and Blandino asked for those flags when the contact was clearly beyond five yards. Grabbing an eligible receiver's jersey was yet another point that the referees were told to focus on. Even if the official did not think that the grab/pull of the jersey had any impact on the receiver or the route they ran, it was still counted as defensive holding. Lastly was a penalty targeted at the offense rather than the defense which was pushing off at the top of a route. This was generally on the bigger bodied receivers who would get to a break point in their route and use a little shove to get that extra bit of separation between them and a defender. Hands to the face got a tighter look at the same time. The last point of emphasis for this season was illegal use of hands which was neither a offense or defense specific penalty but something that was generally pretty evenly split in illegal use of hands. This was defined as: an illegal use of hands penalty in the NFL occurs when a player uses their hands, arms, or body to forcefully contact, push, or hold an opponent in an unauthorized manner. In lame mans speak, this was most commonly called when someone was thrusting their hands into an opponent's head, neck, or face. You'll see it quite common for offensive and defensive linemen as they try to get a handle on each other or perhaps when a running back is trying to stiff arm someone but instead gets under their helmet or neck.  

So there was a huge focus across the board on all these points of emphasis, but did they all come to fruition? Were they impactful in the following seasons? Of course, the NFL isn't going to make a stink of something only to not make any calls throughout the year. Illegal contact went from 37 to 102 penalties that first year, defensive holding increased from 171 to 216, offensive pass interference (pushing off) climbed to 102 from the previous seasons 61, and illegal use of hands doubled going from 74 to 164 penalties on the season. There was yet another spike just as things were getting "back to normal". While these spikes were explosive for these specific calls, it was short lived as the illegal contact came back into orbit dropping from 102 to 57 and illegal use of hands dropped from 164 to 117 in 2015. The 2025 season retained the emphasis on defensive holding and offensive pass interference but also brough emphasis to a new rule for illegal formation.

Due to the plethora of new and adjusting rules over this short period of time, flags were flying left and right as players struggled to grasp what they could and could not do anymore and fine that fine line of legality and foul. The first 3 weeks of the 2015 season saw an average of 15.3 flags a game which is the second most only behind the beginning of the 2005 season, however the yards per game topped out at 130 penalty yards per game which is the highest total all time for a start of the season proving that the flags weren't just abundant, but they were all impactful. Blandino had stated that this was expected as players and refs adjusted and that the calls should level off as the season went on. He was right in some sense as they did not average over 15 penalties a game, but this season ended up as the third most penalized season in modern history again only falling short of those infamous 2004 and 2005 record setting seasons.  

Perhaps the league heard the complains (and boos) from fans as a flag was becoming more common than a third down conversion.  In 2016, it seems as though the calls which were emphases a year or two ago were but mere thoughts in the wind as unnecessary roughness dropped from 229 to 195, illegal use of went from 117 to 89, and roughing the passer lowered to 85 from 101. Though not all of these calls were dropping as pass interference continued to rise and hit a high for this time period at 279 from the previous years 231.  While there were certainly less penalties called in 2016, there was still complaints among coaches and fans that there were plenty of missed hits and sloppy calls. But come the 2017 year, it seemed that not a whole lot changed. Refs cleaned up some calls but across the year, it was pretty similar to the year prior. For the first time in a few years, it appeared that we might have a new normal in the NFL. 

This new normalcy was only enforced when there was yet another emphasis on roughing the passer in 2018. They league was cracking down on when defenders who intentionally landed on QBs with all their body weight, crushed runners who were sliding feet first,  as well as lowering their heads to initiate contact. While the first few weeks of the seasons saw a massive spike of double the calls from previous years, they were cleaned up by week 4 and the rest of the year played on on a similar pace to the previous 2 years. Surprisingly, the 2019 season saw a 4th year of what seemed to be the new norm. The NFL had gone through numerous points of emphasis throughout the past 20 years, and it seemed like everything was finally all ironed out on what were clear fouls and how to play the game properly.
empty:
The year the world shut down, well almost the whole world, because God knows we can't go a season without football. Aside from the social distancing, a new meaning to face mask, and empty stadiums, this was an interesting year in the NFL. Walt Anderson was in his first year as the head of the officiating training and his theme for the year was "clear and obvious" flags only. The goal was to reduce the ticky-tack flags and a lot of the calls that were subjective or had minimal impact on the game. If you've been following along, this was of course on the backside of 2019 which had the most holding calls of all time in a season at 719. It was a directive in 2019 to focus on holding and now it was yet again a focus and point of emphasis, however, this year was in the opposite direction in an attempt to bring those calls back to reality. 

On top of it being the covid year, there was no preseason and they had brought in a large class of new officials compared to previous years. These factors paired with the new focus on reducing holding calls led to one of the lease penalized seasons in the history of the NFL. Holding took an astounding dive from 719 calls the previous year to 459 in 2020 which is the lowest point for holding across this study. Not only on the offensive side was holding reduced, but defensive holding fell from 244 to 168. Certainly not as big of a drop, but still a noticeable reduction.  

If you watched any football in 2020 it was most certainly from your couch because, as I'm sure you recall, stadiums were completely empty aside from a couple carboard cutouts. Believe it or not, this seemed to have an impact on the reduction of penalties as well. All too often we see a team go into an opposing stadium and have trouble with snap count or they end up jumping off sides on a crucial 3rd down due to the stadium pulse being maxed out. Surprisingly though, it was the home team who seemed to benefit the most, having their false start penalties drop from 282 to 232 year over year whereas the opposing teams false start rate stayed about the same. Defensively it was the flip side of the coin where it was the visiting teams who seemed to benefit the most. The road team managed to reduce their offside penalties from 117 to 88 proving that it is much easier to not jump offsides when there isn't a crowd screaming and pressuring the defense to get a good jump. Similarly, home teams ended up increasing their defensive offside rate from 79 to 100 during that whole season. . This can likely be attributed to the opposing QB having a much quieter field and actually having the ability to work their hard count and cadence causing the home favorites to jump more frequently.

It wasn't all sunshine and rainbows this year, as not all calls ended up falling this year.  As seems to be a common narrative throughout this study, the defense seems to get the short end of the stick and their calls very rarely see a reduction in penalties once a point of emphasis is introduced. This was the case for this season as illegal contact again rose a whopping 61% year over year and defensive pass interference hit an all time high of 308 penalties, the highest amount for this penalty type of any completed season in history.
formation:
Under the competition committee run by Walt Anderson, the flags stayed low for a few seasons following 2020. They spiked a bit in 2021 as the holds bounced back up to 656 before dropping back down to a midpoint between that high and the 2020 low.  A handful of penalty calls transitioned ups and downs between each other with illegal contact and false starts increasing again and roughing the passer and defensive pass interference decreasing. The no fun league returned as they made taunting and celebrating a point of emphasis. In this new era, two taunts in a game would sign you up for a swift ejection, Chad OchoCinco and William Gay would never have survived! At the end of the 2003 season, Walt Anderson left the competition committee and the era of minimal flags was in jeopardy as a new figure emerged into the scene. 

Come the 2024 season, Ramon George took over as the vice president of officiating training and development. With his new role, the NFL wanted to focus on the formation and how offenses were lining up. We have to take a peak on the defensive side of the ball to make sense of this though. Edge defenders were getting better as TJ Watt set the single season record for sacks with 22.5 , so in an attempt to stop these agile edge rushers, offensive tackles began lining up as far to the side of the guard and  as far back off the centers midline as they could get away with as a way to gain even a fraction of a step to help prevent a sack. Teams noticed this and so did the league as it became the main focus whereas tackles needed to be on the line of scrimmage and cross their head to at least the centers midline. The league surprisingly gave a lot of grace with this and promised a warning to players before they'd throw the first flag. The league and the officials made a statement on the first week of the new season calling illegal formation 5 times on the Ravens in one game. Across the year this was a highly penalized new rule paired with the illegal shift, another alignment family penalty. 

Across the whole year, illegal formation doubled and then some from the 57 in the prior year to 128 in 2024. Similarly illegal shift nearly doubled from 36 to 61 in the 2024 season. It seems that Ramon George was a bit more penalty happy than the previous Anderson was. Holding which had been referees had been more lenient on (a point of emphasized previously) jumped up from 560 to 682, false starts also brought back the minimal twitch call and rose from 618 to 679. A change in the way kickoffs were now done also added a new element and new rules to follow which obviously were broken 36 times over the course of the year. And of course how can we forget one of the most impactful rules that was added in 2025, the hip drop. There were a handful of high profile players, most notably Mark Andrews, who had some lower leg and ankle injuries from being....tackled, so the NFL implemented a rule where if you tackled a player and your hip happened to swivel around and fall on that players lower legs, which was the case many times when a smaller defender was trying to tackle a TE or RB, this was now a penalizable offense. Over the course of the full season, the NFL saw this event and penalty skyrocket from 0 in the previous years (obviously because it wasn't a penalty) to a whopping, game breaking, season altering 1. Then following the game, the league reviewed the call and determined it should not have even been called a penalty.
epidemic: So a new wave of leaders has entered the building and the penalties are began to rise again. While the season is still young and only 6 weeks deep so far, the 2026 year is looking like it might be on pace to break the record for most penalties ever. It currently sits the second highest average penalties per game through six weeks, only behind 2005 which was the highest penalized season in history. The biggest increases year over year have been offensive holding up 14%, delay of game up 38%, false starts up 10%. While these percentages might not seem too impactful, holding and false starts are the most penalized plays almost every year, so seeing an increase across the board is not a promising site if you are a football purist who likes to just let them play. Maybe we're all overacting as the starts to seasons are always the highest penalized periods over the year, but then again, maybe we aren't and there truly is a flag problem. Based off of the math, we are seeing a flag on just about 12% of all plays meaning 1 out of every 8 plays will see a flag. If your team is lucky enough to get 2 first downs, it's unlikely they got that far without seeing at least one flag on them or the defense to aid in those first downs. I guess only time will tell as this season goes on, but I am not hopeful that the flags will fall and the players will be the ones making the most impacts on the fields.
dive: The analysis above follow one change at a time one season at a time. This part is the more broad view of the league and how penalties are thrown. Does the offense get punished more? When are flags the most common? Where were the spikes in calls? To figure out if we have a flag problem, we have to figure out the who, what, when, where, and why?
pointed: Let's first take a look at the league's calls of emphasis across the years. They were obviously mentioned above, but how do they compare over the years? It seems that quite frequently, the league will point to a call being missed or overcalled, there will be an increase or drop year over year, but then as time goes on, that call seems to slowly creep back to old levels. At least that seems to be the case for illegal contact, Illegal use of hands, Illegal formation, offensive pass interference, and taunting. Defensive flags such as defensive pass interference and defensive holding seem to have stuck though as time has gone on.
volume:
The three most prominent calls throughout the duration of any season are always holding, false starts, and pass interference. These three have to sit on their own chart because they generally sit over 300+ calls every year, whereas the others hardly ever see 200 calls in a year.  In the early 2000s, false starts far outnumbered holding, but in the mid 2010, they flip flopped. In 2020 there was a point of emphasis on offensive holding in an attempt to reduce calls, that season flags fell from an all-time high of 719 to an all-time low of 459. Ever since that point, false starts and holding have bounced back and forth and the two of them now sit around the same rate throughout the season. Defensive holding has always been around but in recent years it seems to be a bit more of a focus as it has been rising and hit an all time high in 2017 and has rivaled that in bot 2021 and 2024. 

Obviously being the three most prominent calls in a season, it is no surprise that when these three go up or down, the average flags per season follow a similar trend. The 2005 season saw highs for both false starts and holdings and an increase from the previous year for pass interference and because of that, it is no surprise that is the highest flagged season of all time.
playoffs:
As we get into the final stretch of the season, with the most important games of the year, how do flags fare? From the looks of it, flags seem to fall when the playoffs hit. It makes sense, obviously the better teams in the league make it to the playoffs, and the best teams in the league likely aren't giving away 100 yards worth of penalties every game. That's one reason, but it could also be that refs want to let the teams play and have as little an impact in the outcome as possible. This is some of the best football of the year and I am personally a fan of the refs letting them play as long as it's nothing egregious or game changing that gets let go. 

That being said, with the flags per game being reduced, it can make every flag feel that much bigger and more impactful. It feels like all too often we have seen a situation where a play has been decided by a pass interference or a hold giving or something that gives one team a second chance or a chip shot at a field goal. I know it's not much, but during the playoffs it averages about 10 penalties a game whereas the Superbowl averages just shy of 12. Maybe that's why there is always some criticism of the Superbowl and officiating because over the previous weeks, the user is spoiled with minimal flags only to see 2 more, generally impactful flags thrown which can all too often determine the outcome of a close game.
sides:
The first question we have to answer when trying to get a better grasp on penalties as a whole is WHO commits the most fouls? When we break down the numbers, we see that it is the offense committing about 7 fouls a game whereas the defense is only committing about 5 fouls a game. This isn't all that shocking as the most common calls in the league are false starts and holding. But what is shocking is that the two are nearly identical in penalty yardage per game. 

The offense is responsible for about 53 yards a game and the defense about 52 yards per game. So while the defense has less fouls in a game, they have the more impactful fouls. Again we can make sense of this because all offensive fouls have a limit of 15 yards for even the most heinous of acts. But defensively, there is one foul that is so violent and so atrocious that they decided there is no limit to the distance and yardage, this of course is pass interference. This foul is moved to the spot of the foul, so if this foul occurred 23 yards down the field, this is a 23 yard penalty. In theory, if you had Uncle Rico back there throwing the ball over the mountain and going 100 yards goal line to goal line and the defender bumped the receiver in the endzone, this could be called for a 100 yard pass interference call.
when_body: Just watching the first few week, it seems that every year starts off hot and heavy with the flags. Whether they are trying to implement a new rule, players are still rusty in their first games, or teams are still figuring out their starting lineup, flags always seem to fly early in the season. The stats hold up with this feeling too, the first few weeks of the season see the highest rates of flags averaging 13.3 in the first 5 games.  Week 6 on averages about 12.3 flags a game and then it continues to fall off even more towards the end of the year in the playoffs when the games matter the most.
where:
Whether it be playoffs or a regular season, everyone and their mother knows being the home team gives you an advantage, right? The crowd at your back, overwhelming support and cheers, local refs, these are clearly all factors that help the home team and hinder the away team. 

While those might not all be completely true, the stats do hold up and it shows that throughout a season, the opposing team is almost always flagged at a higher rate. It may not be a huge gap, generally only about 1 flag difference a game, but when the game is on the line and the crowd is at its loudest, I would hate to be an away team.
discipline:
Which teams are the most penalized across the history of the NFL? While not all flags are avoidable, there are certainly teams that are better than others at showing more discipline. 

The Raiders are have been the most penalized club in this file, 7.32 flags a game across 443 regular-season games. This lines up with the story that has been told, the better teams don't commit as many penalties and the Raiders have been one of the worst teams over the past 27 years. On the flip side, the second least penalized team is the Patriots who averaged 5.67 penalties a game, and during that same time, they have won 6 Superbowls. Follow the penalties and you can likely follow which teams have been good or bad.
contact_deck:
When trying to determine which batters had great seasons or if we are looking to predict into the future, what stats do we want to look at? HRs? RBIs? On base percentage? 

While these are all useful and offer some semblance of clarity to who were efficient hitters, they are all flawed in their own ways. HRs are great, but they usually don't tell the full story of if a hitters season. Were they striking out 9 at bats in a row and then would hit a HR on the 10th at bat? Did they have very few HRs but lead the league in batting average?  The same devils advocate game can be played for RBIs, were they the leadoff hitter who never has a runner on base their first at bat? Or were they batting cleanup and had bases loaded every other at bat? Lastly looking at OBP, did they lead the league in HRs and RBIs, but had a poor batting average striking out almost every other at bat? Or did they have a top tier OBP, but because they walked at least once a game? 

The point of this is, while these may be useful in some respects, none of those metrics are great at helping determine how efficient a hitter was all season. This is where wOBA enters the conversation. Weighted on-base average (wOBA), gives each result of an at bat a weight for the runs it tends to create. An out is 0,  a single is about 0.9, a double is about 1.25, and a home run is 2.0. I say ABOUT, because the scale changes over a full season. The MLB scales those weights so a league-average wOBA perfectly mirrors the league average OBP, which generally sits around .320. So giving a bit of a look into what good vs. bad would be, a .400 or better season is an all-star, MVP season. A .320 is about league average, and a .280 or lower is a guy who may be searching for a new job at the local grocery store next year.
contact_fit: To turn all these numbers in to data, I took all 533,930 balls in play from 2020 through 2024 and looked at it's three measurements, the speed it left the bat, the trajectory angle, and the wOBA statcast gave that ball. To model this, I ran a stack of small decision trees. Each decision tree asks whether the ball was hit harder than some speed, and whether the angle was higher than some degree. The model keeps splitting until the balls in a specific group all look alike. Based off of these designations, I can take any newly hit ball and filter it down these decision tress based on the trajectory angle and the exit velocity to predict the wOBA of this newly hit ball. The guess for a new ball is the average wOBA of the group it lands in.
contact_check:
This graph above is the result showing how each ball was rated based off of trajectory and exit velocity, it was then compared to how it actually played out on the field. The yellow line is my model and the blue line is the MLB statcast expectation for each ball. 

To no surprise, the line stays relatively flat and close to the expected value before a single. These are mostly balls that come off the bat soft or at poor angles which lead them to be expected outs. Of the 52,252 balls with expected contact under 0.2, 92% were outs. 84% of these were your typical fielded out whereas the other 8% were a combination of double plays, sac fly's, fielders choice, or any other out possibility. The remaining 3,964 balls all snuck through in some capacity allowing the batter to get a hit. 2,427 were singles, 629 doubles, 55 triples, 120 HRs, 506 errors, and 227 fielders choice where the batter was safe. 

So of those 52,252 balls expected to score a 0.2 or lower, 0.076 is the average result of what actually happened. This means the 0.076 is the result on the field, The MLB model predicted the result of all of these to be 0.069, slightly closer to 0, an out. My model came in a little high at the expected result of 0.083. This just means that the MLB model gives the fielders slightly more credit for their fielding efforts, while my model predicts the fielders will be slightly more sloppy and have a few more errors.  Interestingly, both models sat only 0.007 off from the actual result showing we are on the right track, just on the opposite side. 

Nevertheless, these were balls that were expected outs, thus it makes sense there was not a whole lot of variation. We begin to see the line diverge when we get past 0.9 and towards the 1.25. This is where the expected results of a swing sits between a single and a double. From 0.9 to 1.1, both my model and statcast are slightly below what actually happened. These balls are the hard line drives, hit around 102 mph and between 15-17 degree angle off the bat. Between the years of 2020-2024, what my model was trained on, these balls averaged 0.945 and my model clocked them at 0.934, slightly lower than the average for those swings during those years. The difference comes because it seems that the defenses adjusted. Balls that were outs 36% of the time from 2020-2024 shifted to being outs 45% of the time in 2025. Defense got better at fielding these balls or adjusting to the batter hitting them. Thus, my models predicted 0.934 weight for the balls between 0.9 and 1.1 was off the mark of the actual weight of 0.868. 

The gap only widens from here as we get towards the hard hit fly balls. Between the 1.3 band and the 1.6 band, we see the biggest gap from my model to the true result. I rate these balls on average about 1.432 so any time one of those balls is a HR it only beats my prediction by 0.56 whereas an out beats me by 1.432. On the flipside statcast is beat on a HR by 0.77 and an out by 1.218. Previously this might have been a good line, since between 2020-2024, 48% of the balls hit between 100-106 mph with a 22-28 degree launch angle left the yard and only 26% resulted in outs. Unfortunately, in the big 2025, on balls hit in that same range, now only 41% cleared the wall and 33% ended up being outs. Thus, since more of these balls ended up as outs rather than HRs, my model is punished heavier for my higher projected wOBA average. Both my model and statcast are off, but they are more on the conservative side to these hard hit fly balls being outs compared to my model which seems to be home run happy, causing a larger gap between my predictions and the results. 

Past the 1.6 mark, the line begins to come back down towards normalcy and the predictions again become to be more accurate. This is of course because these are the balls that are absolutely nuked leaving the bat at an average of 107 mph and around a 27 degree launch angle. Depending on the model used, these balls are hit between 415-420 feet. The 1.75 band has a 74% HR rate and 14% out rate and it only climbs from there for the 1.85 band and 1.95 bands having 85% and 95% HR rates and 8% and 3% out rates respectively. The top tier of these balls are absolutely slammed and as the numbers say, more often than not, these balls are going home with one lucky fan.

Now that we have explored how the balls are hit and rated based off of the exit velocity and angle, we need to see how much a certain other factor effects these balls actual rating. Of course that other factor is the stadium of play. From those balls closest to the 2.0 weight, we judged the average as leaving the bat at about 107 mph and a 27 degree launch angle traveling about 415 feet. Like we said, these balls were absolutely nuked and obviously are a homerun in every park. Except they aren't......these balls fall short of clearing every fence in 4 parks.  That's Fenway, Comercia, Oracle Park, and Coors Field. 

Obviously I'm looking at only the deepest parts of these fields and if the batter hits that same ball to right or left, it is likely a homerun. The park changes how wide that gap for wOBA gets. Across those 3,772 balls between the 1.2 and 1.8 weight in the graph above, the actual result was 0.160 under what my model projected. At Globe Life Field, 46% of the balls in this category were outs, at Petco Park, 42% were. yet at Dodger Stadium, only 10% were outs where 77% left the yard. Same hits, different parks, and different results. 

Below is a graph of a sample of balls from the season showing how they were hit and their results. As you'll notice there are some deep doubles and short home runs, this is all dependent on the ball park. Some marks sit past the foul lines, these are for when a ground ball passes first or third in fair ground and roll foul, and the dot is where the fielder picked it up.  On a similar note, the home runs in foul territory are balls that hooked around the pole and landed in what would have been foul territory. Toggle the filters and play around with the hit type to see which balls were the most egregious home runs or nukes that were robbed from being a HR becasue of the stdaium.

So we just looked at the balls that were absolutely nuked, but what about the others? There are a handful of balls that fell in the wOBA range of 1.6-1.7 and averaged 396 feet. These are well hit balls, but are the ones that can cause a lot of misses for the average. In 18 stadiums, that 396 foot blast is a homerun to both left and right field. That's over half, but just barely, a batters good game or good season can be dependent on where they are playing majority of their games.

A lefty batter who plays half of their games in Fenway might have more homeruns and throw off the wOBA because a pop fly in many stadiums becomes a HR in theirs at only 302 feet to right field. Same could be said for Yankees stadium where right field is only 314 feet from home and only an 8 foot wall. Not saying this is the case all the time, but obviously the field has some factor in HRs vs. outs on different types of hits.

The gold line is the average fence across the whole MLB. It runs 332 feet down the left field line, 403 feet to center, and 328 feet down the right field line. On balls that traveled 330 to 370 feet and stayed fair, if they were hit to left or right field, it was a home run 84% of the time and an out 3% of the time. Center field was not so lucky being an out 46% of the time and a home run 32% of the time. With a little more power behind the ball and it carried 370 to 410 feet, it was a home run to right and left 99% of the time and if hit to center field, it was a home run 92% of the time, with 7% doubles. 

Below are two charts showing the shortest left and rights fields. Corresponding to the chart above, you can connect the dots on some of the home runs that seem pretty short in left or right field. What may be an easy pop out in any other park, escapes over a few of these short fields, especially when the wall is under 10 feet on an already short deck. Fenway gets some leeway there being the shortest left field because the wall towers at a league high 37 feet tall, almost double of the next highest wall of 19 feet. But on the flipside, it is the shortest right field AND has the shortest wall standing at a measly 3 feet tall, making it an easy target for lefties who are pull hitters .

On top of just seeing how the trajectories and exit velocities lead to hits, I was curious to see which pitches were the most dangerous and which areas of the plate lead to the most costly hits for a pitcher. To do this, I looked at only the batted balls that went for and identified the hot spots using a heat map. 

To no surprise, the middle of the plate lead to the most costly hits for a pitcher with the wOBA sitting around 1.2 which translates to an expected double. There was one spot just above the strike zone which had the highest wOBA of 1.27, however, there were only 58 instances in this box which makes it hard to validate since the ones in the middle of the plate have samples of 6 to 7 hundred. 

Another unsurprising point was low balls, and balls in the dirt, were the safest pitches for pitchers. Pitches below the zone would often time only result in a wOBA of around 0.9-1.0 which was about a single. Obviously these are only the hits, so so when you toggle in the "all contact" on the graph, you can see that those numbers plummet. You can also see how incorporating the outs rather than just the hits really brings down the whole wOBA, which is foreseeable since you'll be lucky to see a team get 10 hits in a game whereas 27 outs are guaranteed every game for that same team.
contact_heat_after:
From that data, I was able to create this heatmap below for how a hits trajectory and exit velocity turned into wOBA. As you can see, a ball that is hit off the bat above 105 mph and at an angle between 27-30 degrees is more likely than not a homerun. This is the ideal hit that every batter is looking for. The problem is that it's not that easy, and get just a bit under the ball that could have been a homerun, changes its trajectory and turns into a pop up leading to an out. A ball that was hit 106 mph off the bat, but at a 50 degree angle falls to an expected wOBA of 0.095, almost always an out. 

Obviously any ball hit 0 degrees or below is a ground ball. Any of the little dinky hits that barely eclipse 60 mph are almost guaranteed outs. As expected though, a hard hit ball works magic and if a batter manages to get a hold of one of those poorly angled balls, their wOBA of a ball hit at -4 degrees goes from about 0.104 all the way up to 0.464. Definitely not a hit in many cases but certainly gives them a fighting chance at getting on base. 

The line drives appear to be the safest hit ball which makes sense. Due to the launch angle, they are often times sent over the infielders head and into the outfield. This is why the average for a line drive sits right around 1.0 which is an expected single that can possibly stretch into a double. The line drives that just miss out on being home runs tent to average a bit higher of a wOBA and are closer to a 1.1 or 1.2 meaning they are expected to result in doubles more often then not.
